summary: A first-person neighborhood feature on how a collaborative heritage project, launched by local authorities in September 2023, uses drones, LiDAR, 3D printing, crowdsourced photos, VR and robotics to conserve a historic district's architecture. The author interviews experts and project leaders, who describe non-invasive methods that preserve both the physical structures and the authenticity of their history. The piece concludes that technology is giving shared heritage a new lease on life.
one_line: A local feature on how drones, LiDAR, 3D printing, crowdsourcing, VR and robots are being used to preserve a historic district's architecture since 2023.
key_facts: Local authorities started a collaborative project to conserve architectural treasures with cutting-edge technologies in September 2023.
Dr. Emily Farthington, a leader in architectural conservation tech, uses non-invasive techniques that let bricks and stones tell their own story without being touched by human hands.
The 'Drones for Dome' campaign debuted on October 12, 2023, deploying a swarm of drones to survey and map the oldest domes in the city.
Drone data is accurate to the millimeter and is used to create digital twins of structures as a foundation for restorations and future analyses.
In November, LiDAR technician Michael Richardson demonstrated Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) on the Town Hall façade, which is marred by pollution; he compared it to having X-ray vision.
On December 5, architect Julianne Moore unveiled a 3D-printed replica of a lost 17th-century fountain, recreated stone by stone from scans of similar period pieces and historical records.
The original 17th-century fountain was a victim of urbanization and survived only in etchings and memories.
On February 3, 2024, local historian Johnathan Castro announced the 'Photo Vault of Yesteryears' project, asking citizens for old photographs, memories and anecdotes of neighborhood landmarks.
In March, an immersive virtual reality experience launched, created by Jane Wilson, letting users explore historical buildings as they were centuries ago.
In April, robotics engineer Alexei Petrov demoed a robot performing delicate restoration work on the friezes of the city's old opera house.
Petrov said robots eliminate human error and fatigue and ensure longevity and sustainability, calling this the future of heritage conservation.
Drones with high-resolution cameras and 3D scanning were seen around the spire of the centuries-old St. Andrews Church, pinpointing repairs without physical scaffolding.
